source.title: SONI: Selective Orthogonalisation via Noise Injection

record.file_problem: The text is present, but many equations, symbols, and parameter values are missing from the web rendering. Some results are described in prose while their plotted values are unavailable.
record.tranche_reason: The study develops and evaluates SONI, a fine-tuning method intended to alter feature geometry. Its reported geometry results follow that deliberate intervention; it does not test whether unmodified models naturally exhibit the claim’s proposed representation. It uses Toy Models of Superposition as its setting and motivation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SONI outcomes, including changes in feature orthogonality, performance, and failure at higher expected activations. These are results of the study’s deliberate geometry-altering intervention, not tests of the claim versions about naturally arising representations. The text also discusses SAEs and possible LLM applications as background or future work; it reports no LLM experiments or downstream safety-intervention results.
record.test_reason: The study uses Anthropic's TMS toy model as a testbed for its own fine-tuning method, SONI, which deliberately reshapes feature geometry. All reported results concern SONI's success and its costs: target orthogonality, error, norm and failure under co-activation. The base model's pentagon arrangement (m=2, n=5, parameters copied from TMS) is shown only as a qualitative setup check, with no measurement of the sparsity transition or geometry. That does not amount to a test of V1 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim a theoretical derivation that the noise applies a purely rotational force, preserving feature magnitudes. They frame SONI as a middle ground between full superposition and orthogonalisation methods. LLM application and downstream safety benefits remain unverified.
record.recipe_differences: The study first trains a Toy Model of Superposition, then applies its own targeted-noise fine-tuning method; this is not a reproduction of the original study's method for characterising superposition.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome depends on sparsity or expected activations per input, dimensionality, and targeted-noise hyperparameters. The method is reported to fail above approximately 1 expected activation per input in the n=400 sparsity sweep; sigma changes maximum cosine similarity, test error, and target norm.

fits_no_version.finding: Targeted directional noise during fine-tuning orthogonalises a chosen feature in TMS models (n=5 to 1600) with minimal error cost. It fails when expected activations per input exceed about 1, where the target norm collapses and max cosine similarity degrades.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy superposition models, targeted noise injection can selectively orthogonalise one feature, subject to a co-activation limit tied to input sparsity.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to toy models. The paper reports no LLM experiments or downstream safety-intervention evaluation. Many parameter values and plotted numerical results are unavailable in the text rendering, and no uncertainty estimates are stated.

untested.parts: Only a qualitative pentagon in the base m=2, n=5 model is shown. It notes in passing that low sparsity collapses superposition at small n. There is no measured sparsity-dependent transition and no geometry analysis of unmodified models.
Neuron polysemanticity and capacity competition are not examined. The importance ordering of which features survive is not analysed.
No LLM experiments and no SAE recovery.
SAEs are mentioned only as background. Their completeness, stability and canonicity are not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The base-model pentagon (Fig. 2) incidentally reproduces the original TMS geometry, but only as a qualitative setup check. This is not counted as a test. The remark that low sparsity collapses superposition at small n is also given without data. The intervention is deliberately induced, so its rows bear on no version. Numeric values are missing from the rendering. The source is a LessWrong post, not peer reviewed.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether features in unmodified toy networks naturally form the claimed overlapping, nearly orthogonal geometry, or how that geometry varies with sparsity and importance.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity arises from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
No LLM feature-distribution or SAE-recovery experiments.
SAEs are discussed, but their completeness, stability, or canonical status is not tested.
Does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Anthropic's Toy Models of Superposition (m=2, n=5)
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned with targeted noise in the direction of feature 3 to orthogonalise other features against it.
rows.measure: Maximum cosine similarity between the target feature and other feature vectors
rows.baseline: Original model before fine-tuning; numeric value not stated
rows.value: Near zero after fine-tuning; numeric value not stated
rows.locator: Figure 2; Figures 3–4; Results and Discussion, m=2, n=5 Toy Model
rows.note: The paper describes feature 3 as becoming perfectly orthogonal to surviving features; features 2 and 4 collapse. This is an outcome of the deliberately induced intervention, not evidence of naturally arising geometry.
